mapAttribution: Schematic kingdom/empire extents for Europa Strata — not cadastral or modern state borders. Rings approximate political control at tick years (Euratlas-informed).
narrative: From Hundred Years’ War and Reconquista finales through Italian Wars, Ottoman–Habsburg collision, Reformation fracture, and the Dutch Revolt’s edge—Europe’s map is dynastic and confessional, not national.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.description: Valois France exits the Hundred Years’ War as a bruised but consolidating territorial monarchy. Charles VII and Louis XI claw back English continental footholds and clip Burgundian and feudal autonomy; Brittany is absorbed through dynastic marriage. Sixteenth-century Valois kings fight Habsburgs in Italy and along the Rhine, then tear the realm in the Wars of Religion. Henri IV’s Bourbon settlement (Nantes, 1598) closes the century with a reunited Catholic crown tolerating a Huguenot minority. Royal fiscal-military growth, parlements, and a Paris-centered court culture remake the medieval patchwork into an early modern state—still short of Louis XIV’s later frontiers.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs England (to 1453); Burgundian wars / League of the Public Weal; Italian Wars vs Habsburgs (1494–1559); Habsburg encirclement under Charles V/Philip II; French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) including St Bartholomew; interventions in Scotland and against Spain.
polities.leaders: Charles VI; Charles VII; Louis XI; Charles VIII; Louis XII; Francis I; Henry II; Catherine de’ Medici; Charles IX; Henry III; Henry IV of Navarre/Bourbon.
polities.religion: Catholic monarchy with Gallican royal claims over the French church. Huguenot (Calvinist) minority grows mid-century; Edict of Nantes (1598) grants limited coexistence after decades of confessional civil war.
polities.culture: Late Gothic into French Renaissance courts (Fontainebleau), vernacular chronicle and poetry, printing, and a developing absolutist ceremonial. Occitan south remains culturally distinct under northern political victory.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.description: Lancastrian England opens the century still claiming the French crown and holding Gascony; defeat in France (1453) coincides with the Wars of the Roses. Tudor consolidation under Henry VII/VIII recenters power on a stronger English monarchy, break with Rome, and naval-commercial ambition. Elizabethan England survives Spanish Armada pressure, expands Atlantic venturing, and tightens hold on Ireland. Calais—the last continental bridgehead—falls to France in 1558. Map focus is the island kingdom plus fleeting French footholds, not later British Isles unions.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War; Wars of the Roses; Anglo-Scottish wars; Tudor conquest/plantation pressures in Ireland; war with Spain (Armada 1588); continental interventions in the Dutch Revolt and France.
polities.leaders: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I (James VI/I from 1603).
polities.religion: Catholic to mid-1530s; Henrician/Edwardian Reformation; Marian Catholic restoration; Elizabethan Protestant settlement. Persistent Catholic minority and Puritan pressure within the Church of England.
polities.culture: Chaucerian afterlife into print culture; Tudor court humanism; Shakespearean drama by 1600; vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer reshape literacy and identity.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.description: Stewart Scotland remains an independent kingdom allied by Auld Alliance to France against England. James IV’s disaster at Flodden (1513) and later Reformation turmoil under Mary Queen of Scots reshape the realm. By 1560 Scotland adopts a Calvinist kirk; in 1603 James VI inherits England (personal union), but the kingdoms stay legally separate through 1600’s map year.
polities.conflicts: Border wars with England; Flodden; Rough Wooing; internal magnate feuds; Reformation crisis and Marian civil wars; involvement in French and English politics.
polities.leaders: Robert III; James I–V; Mary of Guise; Mary Queen of Scots; James VI.
polities.religion: Catholic medieval church → mid-century Protestant Reformation (John Knox); Presbyterian kirk structure consolidates after 1560.
polities.culture: Lowland Scots literary culture, Highland Gaelic society, university towns (St Andrews, Glasgow, Aberdeen), and a martial borderer tradition.

polities.name: Crown of Castile
polities.description: Trastámara Castile is the demographic and military engine of the Iberian Reconquista’s final phase. Dynastic crisis and civil war (notably under John II and Henry IV) precede Isabella I’s accession. Union with Aragon (1479) and conquest of Granada (1492) fold Castile into the composite Spanish monarchy; European map after 1500 is carried by the Spain polity.
polities.conflicts: Reconquista vs Granada; civil wars among Castilian nobility; Portuguese border wars; dynastic contests preceding Isabella.
polities.leaders: Henry III; John II; Henry IV; Isabella I (with Ferdinand of Aragon).
polities.religion: Catholic; military orders; large Muslim and Jewish populations under growing pressure culminating in 1492 expulsions/forced conversions.
polities.culture: Castilian vernacular rise, court chronicles, Mudejar artistic hybridity, and crusading frontier ideology.

polities.name: Crown of Aragon
polities.description: A Mediterranean composite crown—Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, Balearics, Sardinia, Sicily, and (from Alfonso V) Naples—oriented to trade and Italian politics as much as Iberia. Ferdinand II’s marriage to Isabella links it to Castile without dissolving separate laws and Cortes; after 1500 the Spanish monarchy entry represents the dynastic union on the map.
polities.conflicts: Italian ambitions vs Angevins and Italian states; Mediterranean rivalry with Genoa and later Ottomans; Castilian alliance/union politics.
polities.leaders: Martin I; Ferdinand I; Alfonso V the Magnanimous; John II; Ferdinand II.
polities.religion: Catholic with significant Jewish and Muslim communities under rising Inquisitorial pressure after union with Castile.
polities.culture: Catalan-Aragonese commercial urbanism, Mediterranean court culture at Naples, and a contractualist political tradition (fueros/Corts).

polities.name: Nasrid Emirate of Granada
polities.description: Last Muslim polity on the Iberian Peninsula, paying parias and playing Castile against itself from the Alhambra. Internal Nasrid factionalism and Castilian-Aragonese unity under the Catholic Monarchs end the emirate in 1492—closing the medieval Reconquista and opening Spain’s Atlantic age.
polities.conflicts: Defensive wars and raids vs Castile; dynastic coups inside the Nasrid house; final war of Granada (1482–1492).
polities.leaders: Yusuf II; Muhammad VII; Yusuf III; Muhammad IX; Abu l-Hasan Ali; Muhammad XII (Boabdil).
polities.religion: Sunni Islam; Mudéjar and Jewish minorities; intense court Sufi and learned culture.
polities.culture: Nasrid architecture (Alhambra), Arabic poetry, and a refined frontier court under existential siege.

polities.name: Spanish Monarchy (Castile–Aragon / Habsburg Spain)
polities.description: Composite Catholic Monarchy forged by Castile–Aragon union, Granada’s fall, American silver, and Habsburg inheritance (Charles V / Philip II). European holdings shown here: Iberia (Portugal after 1580), Italian kingdoms/duchies, and—mapped separately—the Netherlands. Peak power projects against Ottomans, France, England, and Dutch rebels; Armada failure (1588) marks limits of Spanish hegemony without ending the empire. At the 1600 tick Portugal appears as its own polity under Iberian Union rather than being merged into the Spanish fill.
polities.conflicts: Italian Wars; Ottoman Mediterranean war (Lepanto 1571); Dutch Revolt; Anglo-Spanish War; French Wars of Religion interventions; Morisco revolt (1568–71).
polities.leaders: Ferdinand & Isabella; Charles I/V; Philip II; Philip III.
polities.religion: Militant Tridentine Catholicism; Spanish Inquisition; forced conversions of Muslims/Jews; Counter-Reformation patronage.
polities.culture: Siglo de Oro beginnings—painting, mysticism, picaresque prose—funded by American treasure and Italian/Flemish connections; rigid confessional orthodoxy.

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.description: Aviz Portugal pioneers Atlantic exploration—Ceuta (1415), African coasts, Vasco da Gama’s India route (1498), and a seaborne empire of feitorias. European mainland borders stabilize early; power is oceanic. Dynastic crisis after Alcácer Quibir (1578) brings Philip II’s Iberian Union (1580); Portugal remains a distinct legal realm under Habsburgs through 1600.
polities.conflicts: Castilian wars (including 1385 aftermath memory); Moroccan campaigns; competition with Ottomans and later Dutch/English in Asia; 1580 succession war.
polities.leaders: John I; Henry the Navigator (prince); Afonso V; John II; Manuel I; John III; Sebastian; Henry the Cardinal-King; Philip I of Portugal (Philip II of Spain).
polities.religion: Catholic; early Inquisition; Jewish forced conversion (1497) creates New Christian communities central to trade.
polities.culture: Age of Discoveries chronicles (Camões later), Manueline architecture, and a maritime commercial elite oriented to Africa/Asia rather than European land war.

polities.name: Kingdom of Navarre
polities.description: Pyrenean kingdom partitioned by Spanish conquest of Upper Navarre (1512). The rump north of the mountains passes through Foix-Albret to Henry of Navarre, who becomes Henry IV of France—folding Navarrese royal dignity into the French crown.
polities.conflicts: Caught between France and Spain; 1512 Castilian invasion; later French dynastic politics.
polities.leaders: Charles III; Blanche I; John II of Aragon (consort/king); Catherine of Foix; Henry II d’Albret; Jeanne d’Albret; Henry III of Navarre (IV of France).
polities.religion: Catholic south; Jeanne d’Albret’s Calvinism in the north mid-16th c.
polities.culture: Basque-Romance frontier society with strong customary law (fueros).

polities.name: Burgundian State
polities.description: Valois dukes of Burgundy build a dazzling composite between France and the Empire—Flanders cloth cities, Brabant, Holland, and the Burgundian dual duchies—rivalling kings in ceremony and war. Charles the Bold’s death (1477) splits the inheritance: France seizes the duchy; Mary of Burgundy’s Habsburg marriage transfers the Netherlands to Austria/Spain.
polities.conflicts: Armagnac–Burgundian civil war in France; wars with France under Charles VII/Louis XI; Swiss wars (Grandson, Murten, Nancy 1476–77).
polities.leaders: Philip the Bold; John the Fearless; Philip the Good; Charles the Bold; Mary of Burgundy.
polities.religion: Catholic; rich urban confraternities and magnificent court liturgy.
polities.culture: Burgundian court culture—Order of the Golden Fleece, Netherlandish painting, polyphonic music—sets the gold standard for European princely display.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.description: Elective empire of princes, free cities, and ecclesiastical states—not a centralized kingdom. Luxemburg then Habsburg emperors (from Frederick III/Maximilian I/Charles V) try to weld authority while the Reformation fractures confessional unity (Peace of Augsburg 1555). Italian imperial claims fade under French and Spanish wars; Swiss de facto exit. Map shows the German-Central European imperial envelope; major members (Bohemia, Habsburg Austria) are also listed separately.
polities.conflicts: Hussite Wars; Burgundian/Swiss wars; Italian Wars; Schmalkaldic War; Ottoman pressure on eastern borders; princes’ feuds and Peasants’ War (1525).
polities.leaders: Wenceslaus; Rupert; Sigismund; Albert II; Frederick III; Maximilian I; Charles V; Ferdinand I; Maximilian II; Rudolf II.
polities.religion: Catholic imperial idea shattered by Lutheran (then Calvinist) territories; cuius regio after Augsburg.
polities.culture: Imperial diets, university humanism (Erfurt, Wittenberg), print revolution, and a polycentric urban culture from Nuremberg to Cologne.

polities.name: Habsburg Austrian Hereditary Lands
polities.description: Alpine-Danubian core of the Habsburg dynasty—Austria, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, Tirol—from which Maximilian and Charles V build a European dynastic empire. After Mohács (1526) Habsburgs claim Bohemia and ‘Royal’ Hungary; the hereditary lands remain the administrative and military base against the Ottomans.
polities.conflicts: Swiss wars earlier; Ottoman wars after 1526; rivalry with France; internal estate conflicts; involvement in Schmalkaldic and later confessional crises.
polities.leaders: Albert V/II; Frederick III; Maximilian I; Ferdinand I; Maximilian II; Rudolf II.
polities.religion: Catholic stronghold of Counter-Reformation under later Habsburgs; Lutheran pockets among nobles earlier in the century.
polities.culture: Court at Vienna/Innsbruck; Maximilian’s printed self-mythology; Danube fortress society facing the Ottoman frontier.

polities.name: Habsburg Netherlands
polities.description: Seventeen Provinces inherited by the Habsburgs from Burgundy—Europe’s richest urban corridor. Charles V’s birthplace polity becomes Philip II’s tax-and-heresy pressure cooker, exploding into the Dutch Revolt after 1566/1568. By 1600 the north is rebel republic; the south remains Spanish (mapped separately).
polities.conflicts: French border wars; early stages of Dutch Revolt (Beeldenstorm, Alba’s Council of Blood); Calvinist vs Catholic urban strife.
polities.leaders: Philip the Handsome; Charles V; Mary of Hungary (governess); Philip II; Duke of Alba; William of Orange (opposition).
polities.religion: Catholic official; strong Lutheran then Calvinist minorities in cities; Anabaptist episodes.
polities.culture: World-class painting (early Netherlandish → Bruegel), printing, and commercial capitalism centered on Antwerp.

polities.name: Dutch Republic (United Provinces)
polities.description: Northern provinces united by the Union of Utrecht (1579) and Act of Abjuration (1581) fight Spain to a Twelve Years’ Truce (1609, just after our 1600 tick). A Calvinist-led commercial republic with powerful Holland/Amsterdam, federal Estates General, and global VOC ambitions beginning 1602.
polities.conflicts: Eighty Years’ War vs Spain; internal Remonstrant conflicts nascent; naval-commercial rivalry with England/Portugal ahead.
polities.leaders: William the Silent; Maurice of Nassau; Oldenbarnevelt; provincial stadtholders.
polities.religion: Public Reformed (Calvinist) church; substantial Catholic, Mennonite, and Jewish minorities under uneven toleration.
polities.culture: Emerging Dutch Golden Age—cartography, finance, sober urban republican culture distinct from princely courts.

polities.name: Spanish Netherlands (Southern Provinces)
polities.description: Catholic southern provinces reconquered under Parma remain under Spanish Habsburg governors—Flanders, Brabant south, Hainaut—while Antwerp’s trade withers under Dutch blockade. Counter-Reformation baroque culture takes root.
polities.conflicts: Continuation of war with the United Provinces; French pressure on the southern border.
polities.leaders: Alexander Farnese (Parma); Archdukes Albert & Isabella (from 1598).
polities.religion: Restored Tridentine Catholicism; Protestantism largely expelled or underground.
polities.culture: Late Mannerist/early Baroque Flemish art (young Rubens just beginning); court at Brussels.

polities.name: Republic of Venice
polities.description: Maritime oligarchic republic controlling the terraferma of NE Italy plus a shrinking stato da mar (Crete, temporarily Cyprus). Venice fights Ottomans for eastern Mediterranean routes while balancing Italian mainland wars (League of Cambrai disaster 1509). Remains a major independent Italian power through 1600.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman–Venetian wars; League of Cambrai vs most of Europe; Italian Wars maneuvering; War of Cyprus (1570–73).
polities.leaders: Doges (e.g. Tommaso Mocenigo; Francesco Foscari; Leonardo Loredan; Sebastiano Venier after Lepanto).
polities.religion: Catholic with distinctive Venetian church autonomy; Greek Orthodox subjects in colonies; Jewish Ghetto (1516).
polities.culture: Renaissance and Mannerist painting (Bellini, Titian, Tintoretto, Veronese); printing; carnival and civic ritual; Arsenal ship-factory state.

polities.name: Florence / Medici Tuscany
polities.description: Medici banking-republican hybrid becomes the emblem of the Italian Renaissance, then a hereditary duchy under Cosimo I (from 1532; Grand Duchy of Tuscany 1569) within the Spanish-Habsburg Italian system. Territorial expansion absorbs Siena (1555–57).
polities.conflicts: Visconti/Sforza Milanese wars; Pazzi conspiracy aftermath; French and imperial interventions; war for Siena; Savonarolan crisis (1490s).
polities.leaders: Cosimo de’ Medici; Lorenzo the Magnificent; Savonarola (de facto); republican gonfalonieri; Cosimo I; Francesco I; Ferdinando I.
polities.religion: Catholic; Savonarolan theocratic interlude; later Medici Counter-Reformation piety.
polities.culture: Epicenter of Quattrocento art and humanism (Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo, Machiavelli); courtly Mannerism under the dukes.

polities.name: Duchy of Milan
polities.description: Visconti then Sforza duchy—the military prize of the Italian Wars. French occupation (Louis XII, Francis I) alternates with Sforza restorations until Spanish Habsburg rule after the extinction of the Sforza line (1535). Remains the strategic key to northern Italy. From 1535 the duchy is a Spanish Habsburg possession (also reflected under Spain’s Italian holdings).
polities.conflicts: Wars with Venice and Florence; Italian Wars (French vs imperial/Spanish); Battle of Pavia (1525) nearby reshapes European power.
polities.leaders: Gian Galeazzo Visconti; Filippo Maria Visconti; Francesco Sforza; Ludovico il Moro; Massimiliano & Francesco II Sforza; Spanish governors thereafter.
polities.religion: Catholic; Ambrosian rite traditions in Milan.
polities.culture: Late Gothic to High Renaissance patronage (Leonardo at the Sforza court); later Spanish-era conservatism.

polities.name: Papal States
polities.description: Pope as territorial prince over Lazio, Umbria, Marche, and Romagna—restored after the Avignon/Schism era. Warrior-popes (Alexander VI, Julius II) and Counter-Reformation popes (Paul III onward) make Rome again a political and artistic capital while defending orthodoxy against Protestants.
polities.conflicts: Italian Wars coalitions; Cesare Borgia’s Romagna campaigns; conflicts with Venice and Florence; Sack of Rome (1527) by imperial troops.
polities.leaders: Boniface IX; Martin V; Nicholas V; Alexander VI; Julius II; Leo X; Clement VII; Paul III; Pius V; Sixtus V.
polities.religion: Seat of Latin Christendom; Great Schism healed (1417); Council of Trent (1545–63) defines Counter-Reformation.
polities.culture: Renaissance and High Renaissance Rome (Bramante, Michelangelo’s Vatican, Raphael); monumental urban rebuilding.

polities.name: Kingdom of Naples
polities.description: Southern Italian kingdom contested by Angevins and Aragonese; firmly in the Spanish imperial system after the early Italian Wars (Gonzalo de Córdoba’s conquest for Ferdinand). With Sicily, it anchors Spanish power in the Mezzogiorno.
polities.conflicts: Angevin–Aragonese wars; French invasions (Charles VIII 1494, Louis XII); Ottoman coastal raids; baronial revolts.
polities.leaders: Ladislaus of Anjou-Durazzo; Joanna II; Alfonso V; Ferrante I; Spanish viceroys under Ferdinand/Charles V/Philip II.
polities.religion: Catholic; significant Greek-rite and Jewish communities earlier, later pressured.
polities.culture: Aragonese Renaissance court; later Spanish viceregal capital culture; vernacular and Latin learning.

polities.name: Republic of Genoa
polities.description: Ligurian maritime republic, banker to the Spanish crown (asientos), and rival of Venice. Andrea Doria ties Genoa to the Habsburg system after 1528. Territorial footprint small; financial reach enormous.
polities.conflicts: Rivalry with Venice and Aragon; French domination episodes; Corsican revolts; Ottoman naval pressure.
polities.leaders: Doges and oligarchs; Andrea Doria; admiral-princes of the Doria and Spinola houses.
polities.religion: Catholic.
polities.culture: Mercantile oligarchy, Genoese colonial remnants, and palace culture funded by Spanish silver circuits.

polities.name: Duchy of Savoy
polities.description: Alpine buffer state between France and Italy. Emmanuel Philibert recovers lands from French occupation (Cateau-Cambrésis 1559) and shifts the capital toward Turin—launching Savoy’s long climb toward later Italian kingship.
polities.conflicts: French occupations in Italian Wars; wars with Swiss/Bern; maneuvering between Habsburg and Valois.
polities.leaders: Amadeus VIII; Charles III; Emmanuel Philibert; Charles Emmanuel I.
polities.religion: Catholic; Waldensian valleys as persistent dissenting minority.
polities.culture: Alpine feudal-military society evolving into a disciplined early modern ducal state.

polities.name: Byzantine Empire (Palaiologan rump)
polities.description: Palaiologan Constantinople is a shrunken city-empire surrounded by Ottomans, still claiming Roman imperial dignity. The Despotate of the Morea and (separately) Trebizond outlast the City briefly. Mehmed II’s 1453 conquest ends the medieval Roman state on Europe’s political map.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman siege and attrition; civil strife; dependence on Western aid that rarely arrives in force; fall of 1453.
polities.leaders: Manuel II Palaiologos; John VIII; Constantine XI.
polities.religion: Greek Orthodoxy; failed Union of Florence (1439) splits elites.
polities.culture: Last Byzantine humanism; manuscript salvage that feeds the Italian Renaissance; fortress-city mentality.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.description: From Balkan recovery after Ankara (1402) to world empire: Constantinople (1453), Serbia/Bosnia, Hungary’s heartland after Mohács (1526), and Mediterranean challenge to Habsburgs and Venice. Suleiman’s age marks the high tide in Central Europe (Vienna 1529). European map shows Rumelia—the SE European provinces—not the full Asian/African empire.
polities.conflicts: Byzantine conquest; wars with Hungary, Venice, Habsburgs; Mohács; sieges of Vienna; Lepanto (1571); Long Turkish War (1593–1606) underway by 1600.
polities.leaders: Bayezid I; Mehmed I; Murad II; Mehmed II; Bayezid II; Selim I; Suleiman the Magnificent; Selim II; Murad III; Mehmed III.
polities.religion: Sunni Islam (official); Christian millet communities; Jewish refugees from Iberia welcomed; Sufi orders influential.
polities.culture: Devshirme/janissary military society; imperial architecture; multilingual Balkan administration; court at Edirne then Istanbul.

polities.name: Kingdom of Hungary
polities.description: Angevin then Luxemburg/Habsburg/Jagiellon Hungary is a major Central European kingdom until Mohács (1526). Thereafter the map splits: Habsburg Royal Hungary (this polity after 1550), Ottoman central Hungary, and Transylvania (separate). Early ticks show the full medieval realm including Croatia in personal union.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman frontier wars; Hussite spillover; civil wars after Albert/Wladislaus; Mohács; Long Turkish War.
polities.leaders: Sigismund; Albert; Wladislaus I; John Hunyadi; Matthias Corvinus; Wladislaus II; Louis II; Ferdinand I (royal Hungary).
polities.religion: Catholic kingdom with Orthodox minorities; later Protestant nobles in parts; Ottoman Islam in occupied center.
polities.culture: Matthias’s Renaissance court at Buda; military border fortress society; multiethnic Carpathian basin.

polities.name: Principality of Transylvania
polities.description: Eastern Hungarian rump under Zápolya then Báthory princes, vassal to the Ottomans yet a Hungarian-Protestant stronghold. Plays Habsburgs against the Porte; important in the Long Turkish War era around 1600.
polities.conflicts: Hungarian succession wars after Mohács; campaigns with/against Habsburgs and Ottomans; Saxon/Hungarian/Székely estate politics.
polities.leaders: John Zápolya; John Sigismund; Stephen Báthory; Sigismund Báthory.
polities.religion: Early toleration among Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist, Unitarian estates; Orthodox Romanians largely outside the political nation.
polities.culture: Hungarian noble culture, German Saxon towns, mountain principality identity.

polities.name: Lands of the Bohemian Crown
polities.description: Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia, Lusatias—crown lands shaken by Hussite revolution then stabilized under George of Poděbrady and Jagiellons before passing to Habsburgs (1526). A kingdom inside the Empire with strong estates and a Utraquist/Protestant tradition that will explode in 1618.
polities.conflicts: Hussite Wars; wars with Hungary/Matthias; Habsburg consolidation; rising confessional tension by 1600.
polities.leaders: Wenceslaus IV; Sigismund; George of Poděbrady; Vladislaus Jagiellon; Ferdinand I; Rudolf II (court at Prague).
polities.religion: Hussite/Utraquist legacy; Lutheran and Calvinist nobility; Catholic Habsburg court pushing Counter-Reformation.
polities.culture: Czech vernacular religious culture; Rudolphine Prague as late-Renaissance magical-scientific capital.

polities.name: Kingdom of Poland
polities.description: Jagiellon Poland, victorious over the Teutonic Order (Grünwald 1410; Thirteen Years’ War → Royal Prussia 1466), forms a personal union with Lithuania. Nobles’ liberty grows. The 1569 Union of Lublin creates the Commonwealth—thereafter mapped as poland-lithuania.
polities.conflicts: Teutonic wars; Muscovite wars on the Lithuanian front; Ottoman/Moldavian campaigns; succession crises after 1572.
polities.leaders: Władysław II Jagiełło; Władysław III; Casimir IV; John I Albert; Alexander; Sigismund I; Sigismund II Augustus.
polities.religion: Catholic kingdom; Orthodox Ruthenians via the union; Jewish communities; mid-century Reformation among nobles.
polities.culture: Latin and Polish Renaissance (Copernicus), sejm politics, noble republican ideology.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
polities.description: Europe’s largest state by area c. 1400–1500, Baltic to Black Sea approaches, in personal union with Poland. Orthodox Ruthenian majorities under a Lithuanian-Catholic (increasingly Polonized) elite. Loses ground to Muscovy; merges into the Commonwealth in 1569 while retaining a distinct Grand Duchy identity inside it.
polities.conflicts: Teutonic wars; Muscovite wars (incl. 1514 Orsha); Crimean Tatar raids; magnate politics.
polities.leaders: Vytautas the Great; Švitrigaila; Casimir Jagiellon; Alexander; Sigismund Augustus.
polities.religion: Catholic conversion of Lithuanian elite (1387+) over pagan remnants; Orthodox majority in Ruthenian lands; Jewish settlement.
polities.culture: Ruthenian chancery language, Lithuanian dynastic memory, multiethnic noble commonwealth in formation.

polities.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polities.description: Union of Lublin (1569) creates a vast elective noble republic stretching from the Baltic toward the steppe. Around 1600 it is a great power under Sigismund III Vasa, intervening in Muscovy’s Time of Troubles, yet structurally limited by Golden Liberty politics.
polities.conflicts: Livonian War aftermath; wars with Muscovy/Sweden; Ottoman/Tatar frontier; Zebrzydowski rebellion (1606–08) just after tick.
polities.leaders: Sigismund II Augustus (union); Henry Valois; Stephen Báthory; Sigismund III Vasa.
polities.religion: Catholic official culture with 1573 Warsaw Confederation toleration among nobles; large Orthodox, Protestant, and Jewish populations.
polities.culture: Sarmatian noble culture, religious pluralism unusual in confessional Europe, Renaissance/early Baroque hybrid arts.

polities.name: Grand Principality / Tsardom of Muscovy
polities.description: Moscow gathers the Russian lands: absorbs Novgorod (1478), throws off Horde suzerainty (1480), contests Smolensk with Lithuania, and under Ivan IV conquers Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556). Oprichnina terror and Livonian War exhaustion lead into the Time of Troubles after 1598—already looming at the 1600 tick.
polities.conflicts: Wars with Novgorod, Lithuania/Poland, Kazan, Crimea; Livonian War; civil breakdown after Fyodor/Ivan.
polities.leaders: Vasily I; Vasily II; Ivan III the Great; Vasily III; Ivan IV the Terrible; Fyodor I; Boris Godunov.
polities.religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Moscow as ‘Third Rome’ ideology after 1453.
polities.culture: Icon painting, Kremlin rebuilding, chronicles; service-nobility military state expanding into steppe and forest.

polities.name: Novgorod Republic
polities.description: Boyar republic and Hanseatic trade hub controlling the northern forest zone until Ivan III’s annexation (1478) ends its independence—pivotal in Muscovy’s rise.
polities.conflicts: Muscovite pressure and conquest; Teutonic/Swedish frontier clashes; internal veche politics.
polities.leaders: Elected posadniks; archbishops; last independent elites crushed by Ivan III.
polities.religion: Russian Orthodoxy under a powerful archbishop.
polities.culture: Veche republican tradition, birch-bark literacy, fur-trade empire of the north.

polities.name: Teutonic Order / Ducal Prussia
polities.description: Crusading monastic state on the Baltic, humbled by Poland-Lithuania (Grünwald; Second Peace of Thorn 1466 loses West Prussia). Albert secularizes the remnant as Lutheran Ducal Prussia (1525), Polish fief—ancestor of later Brandenburg-Prussia.
polities.conflicts: Polish–Lithuanian wars; Thirteen Years’ War; secularization crisis; vassal obligations to Poland.
polities.leaders: Grand Masters including Ulrich von Jungingen; Albert of Brandenburg.
polities.religion: Catholic military order → Lutheran duchy (1525).
polities.culture: German settler towns, brick Gothic fortresses, militarized colonial Baltic society.

polities.name: Kalmar Union / Denmark–Norway
polities.description: Margaret I’s Kalmar Union links Denmark, Norway, and (uneasily) Sweden. Swedish independence under Gustav Vasa (1523) leaves Denmark–Norway as a Lutheran Baltic power controlling the Øresund tolls.
polities.conflicts: Swedish rebellions; Stockholm Bloodbath (1520); Northern Seven Years’ War; rivalry with Sweden.
polities.leaders: Margaret I; Eric of Pomerania; Christian I–III; Frederick II; Christian IV.
polities.religion: Catholic → Lutheran Reformation under Christian III (1536–37).
polities.culture: Øresund commercial power, Hanseatic interfaces, dual monarchy binding Norway to Copenhagen.

polities.name: Kingdom of Sweden
polities.description: Breaks the Kalmar Union under Gustav Vasa (1523), imposes Lutheran Reformation, and builds a hereditary Vasa state. By 1600 Sweden contests the eastern Baltic under Charles IX—prelude to Gustavus Adolphus.
polities.conflicts: Liberation war vs Christian II; Dacke War; Livonian War; rivalry with Denmark and Poland (Vasa feud).
polities.leaders: Sten Sture (regent); Gustav Vasa; Eric XIV; John III; Sigismund (brief); Charles IX.
polities.religion: Lutheran state church after 1527; Catholic Vasa branch (Sigismund) rejected.
polities.culture: Vasa centralization, Bible vernacular, martial society turning toward Baltic empire.

polities.name: Swiss Confederation
polities.description: Expanding Eidgenossenschaft defeats Burgundy (1476–77) and wins practical independence from the Empire after the Swabian War (1499). Reformation splits Catholic and Protestant cantons (Kappel) without destroying the confederation. Famous export: mercenaries.
polities.conflicts: Burgundian Wars; Swabian War; Italian mercenary campaigns; Kappel Wars (1529–31).
polities.leaders: Cantonal elites; reformers Zwingli and Calvin (Geneva allied); no single monarch.
polities.religion: Split: Catholic forest cantons vs Reformed Zürich/Bern/Geneva orbit.
polities.culture: Communal republicanism, alpine military reputation, urban Reformed intellectual culture (Geneva).

polities.name: Ireland (Lordship / Tudor Kingdom & Gaelic polities)
polities.description: English Lordship is effectively a Pale around Dublin amid Gaelic and Hiberno-Norman lordships until Tudor reconquest. Henry VIII’s Kingship Act (1542), plantations, and the Nine Years’ War (1594–1603) climax around 1600 with Hugh O’Neill’s rebellion.
polities.conflicts: Gaelic resistance; Kildare rebellions; Desmond Rebellions; Nine Years’ War; Spanish intervention at Kinsale (1601).
polities.leaders: English deputies; Earls of Kildare; Hugh O’Neill; Red Hugh O’Donnell; Mountjoy.
polities.religion: Catholic island under Protestant Tudor state religion after Reformation.
polities.culture: Gaelic learned orders and cattle-lord politics alongside Old English towns; cultural conquest accelerates late century.

polities.name: Crimean Khanate
polities.description: Ottoman vassal Tatar khanate controlling Crimea and raiding deep into Poland-Lithuania and Muscovy. Successor fragment of the Golden Horde’s western wing; essential to Black Sea steppe dynamics.
polities.conflicts: Raids on Muscovy and Lithuania/Poland; wars coordinated with Ottomans.
polities.leaders: Hacı I Giray; Mengli I Giray; later Giray khans under Ottoman suzerainty.
polities.religion: Sunni Islam.
polities.culture: Steppe nomadic-aristocratic society with fortified coastal cities and slave-trade economy.

polities.name: Principality of Wallachia
polities.description: Danubian principality oscillating between Hungarian and Ottoman suzerainty. Vlad III Țepeș’s resistance becomes legend; by 1600 Wallachia is an Ottoman tributary with brief assertive moments (Michael the Brave c. 1600).
polities.conflicts: Ottoman wars and tribute politics; Hungarian overlordship contests; Michael the Brave’s unification attempt (~1600).
polities.leaders: Mircea the Elder; Vlad Dracul; Vlad Țepeș; Neagoe Basarab; Michael the Brave.
polities.religion: Romanian Orthodoxy.
polities.culture: Orthodox princely courts, fortified monasteries, frontier military society.

polities.name: Principality of Moldavia
polities.description: Eastern Carpathian–Dniester principality under Stephen the Great resists Ottoman absorption longer than many neighbors, then becomes a tributary. Cultural flowering of painted monasteries; caught between Poland, Hungary, and the Porte.
polities.conflicts: Wars with Ottomans, Wallachia, Hungary, and Poland; vassalage struggles.
polities.leaders: Alexander the Good; Stephen III the Great; Petru Rareș; later Ottoman-appointed princes.
polities.religion: Romanian Orthodoxy; famous Bucovina monastic art.
polities.culture: Orthodox monastic culture, boyar politics, and a buffer identity between steppe and Carpathians.

polities.name: Golden Horde (late / Great Horde)
polities.description: Fragmenting Jochid successor still claiming suzerainty over Rus’ princes into the 15th century. Great Stand on the Ugra (1480) symbolizes Muscovy’s emancipation; the Great Horde collapses by 1502 as Crimea and other khanates inherit the steppe.
polities.conflicts: Internal succession wars; Timur’s earlier devastation aftermath; wars with Muscovy and Lithuania; rivalry with Crimean Khanate.
polities.leaders: Tokhtamysh (earlier); various late khans of the Great Horde; Akhmat Khan (Ugra 1480).
polities.religion: Sunni Islam (since 14th c.).
polities.culture: Steppe imperial remnants, tribute politics, and Turko-Mongol aristocratic tradition.
